title: The headless giant
hookLine: a headless giant grabs the brothers, and someone inside it is glad to see Rama
carry: the self is not the body
last: A SON'S RITES FOR A BIRD.

lines: NO HEAD, A MOUTH IN ITS BELLY.
cards: The brothers head on through deep forest, and the forest gets stranger. Then the path is blocked by something Valmiki describes like a nightmare. It's as big as a hill.
It has no head and no neck. Its mouth is in its belly, huge, with teeth. A single eye sits in its chest.
And its two arms are so long they sweep the forest around it for anything to eat. Before the brothers can turn, those arms close around them both.

teach.b: Its name is Kabandha, and as an ordinary Sanskrit word, kabandha means a headless trunk. The creature squeezes them and says plainly: you'll do for my dinner. Lakshmana is frightened, and Valmiki lets him be.
Leave me as its food, he tells Rama; save yourself, and go find Sita. Rama won't hear of it.

teach.h: TWO ARMS CUT; THE MONSTER IS GLAD.
teach.b: The brothers see it at the same moment: the creature's whole strength is in those arms. Rama cuts off the right arm and Lakshmana the left, and the giant crashes down. Then the strange part.
Lying there armless, the creature asks who they are, and when he hears it's Rama, his whole tone changes. He's glad. He's been waiting for this, he says.
He wasn't always this shape. Under the scene sits one of Hinduism's biggest teachings: the body is not the self.

teach.h: ATMAN: THE SELF IS NOT THE BODY.
teach.b: Inside every body, Hindus teach, is the atman, the real self, which isn't born and doesn't die.

In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna gives it a picture: as a person throws off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, the self leaves worn-out bodies and takes on new ones. So the horror on the path is a body, a covering.
Someone is inside it, and that someone knows Rama's name. It's why, when someone dies, Hindus pray: may his atma find peace. The body is gone; the self has gone on.

how: Artists usually draw Kabandha as Valmiki describes him: headless, with a mouth in his belly. Hindu teachers often explain cremation through the teaching that the atman has left the body, and verses of the Bhagavad Gita are often read at funerals and prayer meetings.

o: a headless trunk, all arms and belly, waiting for Rama
a rakshasa general sent by Ravana to guard the road
a forest serpent that swallows travelers whole

games.q: the thing on the path — tap the pairs.
p: the self that isn't born and doesn't die
the Gita's picture of the body

s: Lakshmana offers himself so Rama can escape
he tells Rama to leave him and go find Sita; Rama won't.
Hindus teach that the self ends when the body dies
the atman isn't born and doesn't die; the Gita says it leaves a body like worn-out clothes.
Kabandha is angry when he learns who they are
he's glad: he's been waiting for Rama.

games.q: Sam asks if Hindus cremate because the person is just gone. what's the Hindu answer?
o: yes, once the body's gone, that's all there was.
the body is a covering; the self, the atman, has gone on.
it's only about custom; there's no belief behind it.
games.why: Hindus teach the atman isn't the body. Kabandha's body was a horror, and someone inside it was glad to see Rama.

practice: Sit still and feel your body: the weight on the chair, your hands, your breath. Then notice the one who is noticing. Many Hindu teachers give this as a simple meditation: the body is felt, and you are the one feeling it.
Breathe in: this is my body. Breathe out: and I am more than it. If you pray, rest in that for a few breaths; if not, simply watch.

wordCard.voice: Kabandha. A headless trunk, all arms and belly, with someone inside waiting for Rama.

orig.note: Sanskrit kabandha: a headless trunk, a body without a head.

carryVoice: Your line: the self is not the body. Tomorrow, the monster tells his story. Day five hundred seventy-six, done.
